title: Bonaventure's journey
hookLine: a Franciscan maps the mind's road to God, starting from creatures

cards: A footprint in wet sand. Nobody's there, but you can tell someone walked this way, which direction they went, maybe how fast. The print isn't the person.
It points to the person. A Franciscan friar named Bonaventure, who led Francis's brothers, went up the mountain of La Verna to pray, and there, he says, he began to map the mind's way up to God.
In that map the whole world is like the sand: covered in footprints, every creature a trace of the one who made it. He wrote it as a short book, step by step.

teach.b: Its Latin title is Itinerarium mentis in Deum: the mind's journey into God.

Bonaventure says the plan came to him on La Verna, as he thought about the six-winged seraph Francis saw there, so he builds the road as six steps, like six wings. The first steps start with what you can see and touch.
Bonaventure calls creatures vestigia, footprints. Their size, their beauty, their order all point back to their maker.
He leans on Saint Paul, who writes in the Douay-Rheims: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made."
A leaf, a river, a sparrow: not God, but a print that says God passed this way. The middle steps turn inward.

Your own mind, which remembers, understands and loves, Bonaventure calls an image of God, a mirror rather than a footprint. Look at how you know and love things, and you are looking at a likeness of the one who made you.
The final steps go beyond both, and here the map turns.

teach.h: AT THE TOP: GRACE, NOT LEARNING.
teach.b: At the top of the road, he says, ask not for learning but for grace, not for understanding but for desire, not for a teacher but for the bridegroom.

teach.h: CLEARLY SEEN, BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.
teach.b: The journey that began with careful study ends in prayer, in silence, in love. Francis praised brother sun; his follower drew a map from the same world.

how: Franciscans read Bonaventure's Journey of the Mind into God as a guide to prayer, and Catholics honor him as a saint and Doctor of the Church.

o: a pilgrim route across Italy to Assisi
a map of the mind's road up to God
a travel diary from a friar's trip to Rome

p: an image of God, a mirror

s: Bonaventure taught that creatures are God
they are footprints that point to God, not God.
Bonaventure says the plan for the book came to him on La Verna
as he thought about the six-winged seraph that Francis saw there.

games.q: you're Bonaventure, at the top of your map. a student asks what to study next to reach God. what do you tell him?
o: ask for grace, not learning; desire, not understanding.
go back and look at creatures again.
games.why: he ends the journey past study: grace, desire, prayer, the bridegroom rather than the teacher.

practice: Choose one living thing near you, or one you remember clearly: a weed in a crack of the sidewalk, a dog asleep, a bird from this morning.
Look at its shape, its order, the fact that it's here at all, and ask, without hurrying, what it's a footprint of. If you pray, let the looking become thanks.

wordCard.voice: Bonaventure's journey. The Franciscan map of the mind's road to God, from creatures as footprints, to the mind as a mirror, to grace beyond them both. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a footprint or trace. Bonaventure's word for creatures that point to God.

carryVoice: Your line: through creatures to God. The road runs from the world, through the mind, to grace. Day eight hundred fourteen, done.
